summary: New construction is taxed in Arizona under the prime contracting classification on 65% of the contract price; additions and remodels of existing property are taxed that way only when the alteration exceeds the statutory threshold, otherwise they are nontaxable MRRA work (the contractor pays tax on materials).

conditions.when: New ('ground up') construction, grading or demolition, or an alteration whose contract amount exceeds 25% of the property's full cash value (residential and certain other property) or $750,000 (other property): taxable at the full rate on 65% of the gross contract (a 35% deduction), state, county and city
Alteration of existing property at or under those thresholds, or replacement of a component or system (e.g. a new roof): MRRA, not taxed to the owner; the contractor pays retail tax on its materials

citations.quote: All construction contracting gross income subject to the tax and not deductible herein shall be allowed a deduction of thirty-five percent (35%).

notes: The 'taxable' outcome is on a reduced base: tax = rate x 65% of the gross contract (A.R.S. § 42-5075(B); MCTC § 415(b)(2) gives cities the same 35% deduction); this rule's 'taxable' does not carry the base. Contracts with a public agency primarily for surface or subsurface land improvements are prime contracting even if they would be MRRA (§ 42-5075(Q)). The MRRA exclusion dates from 2015 (2014 legislation); 2016-12-01 is the edition date of Pub 603 (Dec 2016), the earliest dated ADOR statement read here. No change to the 65% base or the alteration thresholds since 2018 was found.

summary: Maintenance, repair and replacement work on existing property, sold to the owner, is not taxed under Arizona's prime contracting classification; the contractor pays retail tax on its materials and does not charge TPT to the owner.

citations.quote: The gross proceeds of sales or gross income derived from a contract with the owner of real property or improvements to real property for the maintenance, repair, replacement or alteration of existing property is not subject to tax under this section if the contract does not include modification activities, except as specified in this subsection.

citations.title: ADOR Contracting Guidelines, Contracting FAQs
citations.quote: No, labor is not taxable and a contractor's invoice for MRRA projects should not include a line item for tax as neither the labor or the materials are taxable (although a contractor will pay tax on the materials when they are purchased).

citations.title: Model City Tax Code § 415, Construction Contracting (ADOR)
citations.quote: The gross proceeds of sales or gross income derived from a contract with the owner of real property or improvements to real property for the maintenance, repair, replacement or alteration of existing property is not subject to tax under this Section if the contract does not include modification activities, except as specified in this paragraph.

notes: 'Exempt' is the owner's bill: the contractor's materials bear retail TPT (or its equivalent) when bought or used, as a cost of doing business. Maintenance, repair and replacement have no dollar threshold (only alterations do). A contract that also includes more than de minimis modification work is prime contracting. Public-agency land-improvement contracts (§ 42-5075(Q)) are taxable. The exclusion dates from 2015; 2016-12-01 is Pub 603's edition date.

No ADOR page read here names legal, accounting or engineering specifically. Advertising: some cities tax 'local advertising' (MCTC § 405, the media's charge), but an agency's retained commission and fees are excluded. Interior design: goods the designer sells are taxable retail; only the design fee is covered here. Architectural or engineering services inside a construction contract are excluded from prime contracting (A.R.S. § 42-5075(L)).

citations.quote: The tax rate shall be at an amount equal to _______ percent (___%) of the gross income from the business activity upon every person engaging or continuing in the business of leasing, licensing for use, or renting tangible personal property for a consideration, including that which is semi-permanently or permanently installed within the City as provided by Regulation.

notes: No statute names SaaS; ADOR's position rests on letter rulings (LR 11-011, LR 17-001) that the customer's control of the software makes it a rental of tangible personal property. LR 17-001 is a taxpayer information ruling binding only on its requester; 2017-01-03 is its date, not an effective date. The Court of Appeals upheld this treatment in the ADP case (2023; not cited here, a court opinion). Cities tax it under their rental classification (MCTC § 450), whose rates can differ from retail rates. Personal property rental receipts don't count toward a remote seller's economic-nexus threshold, so an out-of-state SaaS seller may not be required to collect.

citations.title: Model City Tax Code § 462, Retail Sales: Food for Home Consumption (ADOR)
citations.quote: the tax must be applied uniformly with respect to all food, and an additional tax or fee differential may not be assessed or applied with respect to any specific food item.

notes: Arizona's city transaction privilege taxes follow the Model City Tax Code, and each city chooses whether to tax food for home consumption (MCTC § 462) and at what rate; a city that doesn't tax it has a 0% food rate. A city's food-for-home-consumption rate can differ from its general retail rate, so a 'taxable' city answer here means taxable at that city's food rate, which this rule does not carry. County excise taxes follow the state base. Which cities tax food on a given date is in ADOR's city rate tables (business code for food for home consumption), not modelled here. HCR 2021 (2025), a referral to the November 2026 ballot that would cap city taxes on food for home consumption, was not in force when this was written and is not modelled. MCTC § 462(f) requires a city food tax to apply uniformly to all food, so a city cannot tax candy differently from other food.

citations.quote: Examples of tangible personal property include, but are not limited to: digital images, handmade items, vehicles, clothing, handmade jewelry, etc.

notes: Undated current official pages: use 1994-01-03, the existing Arizona goods.general rule baseline, as instructed for undated sources; this is not a newly verified historical clothing enactment date. summary: Alcohol sold to take away or served on premises is taxable under the applicable retail or restaurant TPT classification. Separate liquor luxury taxes are not included.

citations.title: ADOR Liquor Luxury Tax — TPT
citations.quote: Licensed liquor retailers in Arizona including farm wineries, microbreweries and craft distillers located in the United States are liable for transaction privilege tax (TPT) when selling spirituous, vinous or malt liquor within Arizona.

citations.title: A.R.S. 42-5074(A), Restaurant classification
citations.quote: The restaurant classification is comprised of the business of operating restaurants, dining cars, dining rooms, lunchrooms, mobile food units, lunch stands, soda fountains, catering services or similar establishments where articles of food or drink are sold for consumption on or off the premises.

citations.title: A.R.S. 42-5074(B), Restaurant classification
citations.quote: The tax base for the restaurant classification is the gross proceeds of sales or gross income derived from the business.

notes: Undated current official pages use the existing goods.general baseline 1994-01-03; this does not establish the historical enactment of alcohol taxation. Retailers and restaurants use different TPT classifications, but both have general taxable treatment. State, county and city rates vary; no different local alcohol sales-tax base was established. Luxury tax is a separate excise, generally imposed at the wholesale tier, and is not modeled.

summary: Renting tangible goods is taxable under Arizona’s personal property rental classification of transaction privilege tax.

notes: No general short/long-term split for ordinary equipment. Publication reports combined state/county rates and city reporting separately. Specialized equipment and exempt-entity exclusions are outside ordinary rental examples. Motor-vehicle surcharges are not modeled.
